text: Beacon is a personal interview coach designed to help people prepare for interviews across different careers. The product description names analytical chemists, ICU nurses, teachers, brand designers, and software engineers as examples, so its intended scope is not limited to one technical profession. A candidate begins by identifying the role they are working toward. Beacon then uses that goal to organize skill expectations, practice activities, feedback, and preparation progress. The central product idea is to make interview preparation feel like a guided process rather than a collection of disconnected question lists. Its coaching is tied to the candidate's stated goal and the information they have provided.

Beacon's product description groups its work into several connected capabilities: building a role-specific skill blueprint, generating short daily practice, reviewing answers with specific feedback, supporting spoken mock interviews, and conversing as a coach that knows the candidate's goal and progress. The product also describes spaced repetition, which brings skills back for review as recall fades. These capabilities serve different moments in preparation, but they are intended to reinforce one another. A skill identified during onboarding can become a practice topic, appear in a preparation plan, and later be revisited as the candidate records progress.

Beacon emphasizes a supportive preparation environment. The product README describes private-by-default use, no public leaderboards, a gentle mode for difficult days, streaks that forgive rest days, and reminders that are sent only when a person opts in. These design choices are relevant to interview preparation because candidates may be anxious, busy, or recovering from a disappointing interview. The product is framed as a personal coach rather than a competitive ranking platform. A useful response should therefore focus on the candidate's next practical step and avoid shaming language, unsupported judgments, or comparisons with other users.

Beacon separates a login identity from a career-preparation profile. The CandidateProfile model has a one-to-one relationship with the configured Django user model, so each login has one career profile. The profile stores the human-readable target role and can also store a list of target roles. It includes interests, an optional target company, an experience level, and a plain-text resume summary. This separation lets the application change career-preparation information without changing the authentication user record. In retrieval answers, the distinction matters: the account identifies who is signed in, while CandidateProfile describes what that person is preparing to do.

CandidateProfile includes preparation constraints that influence the roadmap. A candidate can provide a target interview date, a preparation timeline in weeks, and an optional primary concern. The timeline defaults to six weeks and is validated from one to fifty-two weeks. Primary concerns include technical rounds, behavioral questions, resume and elevator pitch, confidence under pressure, and limited preparation time. The profile also stores the selected experience level, such as current student, new graduate, early career, mid-career, career changer, or returning to work. These fields give Beacon context for tailoring preparation rather than treating every candidate as if they had the same background or deadline.

The resume information in CandidateProfile can be stored as a plain-text resume summary and as an uploaded resume file. The model help text explains that the parser turns the plain-text resume into an initial skill list. Resume information is therefore an input to identifying a candidate's experience, not proof that the candidate has mastered every skill mentioned in a document. Beacon should connect extracted evidence to a shared skill catalog and allow assessment to provide a more structured picture. The target role and resume serve different purposes: the role defines the preparation destination, while the resume supplies evidence about the candidate's starting point.

Beacon's role blueprint describes the skills that interviews for a target role are likely to test and the expected bar for each skill. The README identifies the blueprint as a core product feature and notes that the role-to-skills mapping is cached per role across fields. In practice, the blueprint gives preparation a reference point: it describes what the candidate is working toward before Beacon compares that bar with the person's current evidence. It should be interpreted as a preparation guide, not a guarantee that every employer will ask the same questions. Different companies and interviewers can emphasize different skills, even for the same job title.

The Skill model stores a competency as a shared catalog entry rather than leaving every assessment to invent its own skill wording. Each skill has a name, category, optional description, and creation timestamp. Categories include technical, behavioral, domain knowledge, and communication. The catalog is important because candidates can then be compared against consistent skill labels and target-role requirements. A uniqueness constraint prevents the same skill name from appearing twice within one category, while still allowing a label such as Storytelling to exist in more than one category. This design supports organized diagnosis and consistent links between skills, assessments, and preparation tasks.

Beacon's preparation logic uses the difference between a candidate's current proficiency and the level expected for a target role to identify skill gaps. The README describes a ranking function that considers urgency, gap, market demand, cohort difficulty with Bayesian shrinkage, and exploration when ordering skills for the day's work. CandidateProfile can also store multiple target roles; its model help text says requirements use the highest bar among them. These details mean that the next recommended skill is not necessarily the lowest self-rating alone. Deadline pressure, role requirements, and the product's ranking logic can all affect which skill receives attention first.

SkillAssessment records the relationship between one candidate and one catalog skill. It stores a proficiency score from zero to one hundred, the required level for the target role, the date of assessment, and optional notes. The required level defaults to seventy, and both values are validated on the same zero-to-one-hundred scale. A uniqueness constraint permits one current assessment per candidate and skill, so taking the quiz again updates the current record instead of accumulating duplicate current scores. The model's gap property is the required level minus proficiency, with negative values floored at zero. A positive gap therefore represents remaining preparation work.

Beacon describes skills diagnosis as an adaptive quiz that measures what a candidate can currently demonstrate. The SkillAssessment model documents the result as the candidate's proficiency for one skill compared with the level required by the target role. This distinction is important: proficiency is the candidate's current demonstrated level, while required_level is the benchmark for the role. The difference is used by the plan generator to create tasks. An assessment is therefore more than a quiz score displayed in isolation; it becomes structured evidence that can guide the next preparation activities and later progress review.

CandidateProfile exposes readiness_percent as a derived property rather than a separately stored value. It takes the assessments for that candidate, calculates proficiency divided by required level for each skill, caps each ratio at one, averages the ratios, and converts the result to a percentage. If there are no assessments, readiness is zero. Capping each skill at one prevents a very strong result in one area from hiding an unmet requirement in another area. If a required level is zero, that assessment contributes a ratio of one. The calculation measures progress against recorded skill requirements; it is not a prediction that an employer will make a particular hiring decision.

PreparationPlan represents a time-boxed roadmap for one candidate. It stores a title, the role being prepared for, start and target dates, a status, and whether the plan was generated by AI. A candidate can have multiple plans, for example one for each target role or a regenerated plan after an unsuccessful interview. The target date cannot be earlier than the start date, and a candidate cannot have duplicate plan titles. Plans are ordered by target date so the nearest deadline appears first. The model also derives the plan's total weeks and current week from the date range and today's date.

PlanTask is the concrete action unit inside a preparation plan. A task belongs to one plan and may link to the skill gap it is intended to close. Its fields include a title, week number, instructions, rationale, optional due date, estimated minutes, priority, status, and completion date. Priority is represented as low, medium, or high, while status can be to do, in progress, done, or skipped. The task model constrains week numbers to a defined range and estimated duration to five through six hundred minutes. The rationale field records why Beacon selected the task and can explain a recommendation to the candidate.

PreparationPlan derives completion_percent from its tasks. The property counts all tasks, counts those whose status is done, and returns the completed share as a percentage; an empty plan returns zero. PlanTask ordering groups tasks by week, then higher priority, due date, and title, so a candidate sees an organized roadmap. The plan also derives its current week by comparing the current date with its start date and clamps that value to the plan's total duration. These properties make the roadmap a live view of progress rather than a static list of recommendations. The task records provide the detail behind the overall progress figure.

Beacon encourages short, regular practice rather than relying only on a long session immediately before an interview. The README describes ten minutes of daily practice and questions written fresh for the individual each time. The question is connected to the candidate's goal and preparation needs, and the resulting response receives specific feedback and a stronger example answer. This daily loop creates repeated opportunities to retrieve and explain knowledge. It also gives Beacon new evidence about what the candidate can demonstrate, which can inform later coaching and preparation activities. The ten-minute description is a product design goal, not a claim that every task must take exactly ten minutes.

Beacon reviews written interview answers and can break a response down using the STAR structure: Situation, Task, Action, and Result. The model-selection work includes examples where a strong answer describes the situation, the person's responsibility, concrete actions, and a measurable outcome. It also includes weak examples that are vague or stop before explaining what changed. A good review should distinguish a detailed action from a demonstrated result; word count alone does not establish answer quality. Feedback should identify missing evidence and offer a stronger example answer without inventing achievements or details the candidate did not provide.

Beacon includes a mock interviewer designed for spoken rehearsal. The product description says the mock interviewer listens, asks follow-up questions, and then breaks the candidate's answers down by STAR. It also rewrites the weakest answer in the candidate's own words. The goal is to help a person practise responding in a conversational setting rather than only editing text on a page. The follow-up behavior matters because a real interview is interactive: an initial answer may lead to a request for clarification, evidence, or a more specific result. A useful debrief should connect observations to concrete ways the candidate can improve the next attempt.

Beacon describes a forgetting-curve feature that brings each skill back for review just before recall is expected to fade. The README says the application uses spaced repetition and that the skill-memory component is due at eighty-five percent recall. This makes review timing part of the preparation experience: a skill may return for practice even after the candidate has moved to a different topic. The objective is to revisit information at a useful interval instead of asking the candidate to repeat everything every day. The exact forgetting-curve implementation is represented in the product's studio code, while the project README summarizes its user-facing purpose.

Beacon's coach chat is described as a conversation with a coach that knows the candidate's goal and numbers. The system-design README also identifies the chat feature as grounded in the person's own progress. This context distinguishes the coach from a generic chatbot: an appropriate response can refer to the candidate's stated target role, recorded assessments, plan, or practice history when those facts are supplied to the conversation. The coach should not pretend to know information that is absent from the profile. When the record is incomplete, the response should make that limitation clear and ask for the missing evidence instead of fabricating personal details.

Beacon's data model connects practice work to progress evidence. PlanTask can have TaskAttempt records, and each attempt stores the kind of activity, the submitted response, a score, whether it passed, feedback, the grading method, and optional before-and-after ratings. The TaskAttempt documentation explains that a task is considered done when an attempt passes, rather than merely when a checkbox is selected. The record therefore preserves evidence behind progress and can show how demonstrated performance changes a skill rating. This is more informative than treating task completion as a self-reported click with no associated work or result.

Beacon sends candidate-controlled text, such as resume content and written interview answers, to AI features. The model-selection design places this text inside a clearly marked data block and instructs the model to treat it as information rather than as instructions. The system prompt defines the model's role, task, constraints, output format, safety boundary, and response length. This separation is intended to reduce prompt-injection risk when a resume or answer contains text such as a command to ignore previous instructions. The model should continue performing the requested Beacon task and should not let embedded user content replace the system rules.

Beacon validates model replies before showing them to a candidate. The README names JSON schemas, score ranges, and HTML escaping as validation controls; it also limits allowed formatting to bold text and bullets. The A6/A7 system-design work treats valid structure and instruction adherence as separate criteria. A syntactically valid JSON object can still contain an invented skill, an out-of-range score, or content that violates the requested format. Validation therefore checks more than whether JSON parsing succeeds. If a reply does not meet the expected shape or range, the application should use its fallback or handle the failure rather than displaying unchecked model output.

The Beacon README states that every AI call has a fallback. When AI is disabled through LLM_ENABLED=false, features fall back to transparent, field-neutral rules, which is how the project's tests run. The README also says every model reply is validated before it is displayed. These are complementary controls: fallback behavior keeps a feature from depending entirely on a successful model response, while validation prevents malformed or unsafe output from reaching the interface. For the RAG coach, a similar principle means that retrieval failure or missing evidence should produce a clear limitation message rather than an answer that pretends the knowledge base contains information it does not have.

Beacon is built with Django 5, server-rendered pages, and vanilla JavaScript, with no frontend build step. The README maps product responsibilities to modules: the blueprint creates role-to-skill expectations, the engine calculates readiness and ranks work, cards creates questions and feedback, interview handles mock-interview turns and STAR reporting, chat supports progress-grounded coaching, and reminders handles opt-in nudges. A support console provides diagnosis, problem reports, error logging, and an append-only audit trail. The original preparation application contains profiles, skills, assessments, plans, public API endpoints, charts, and coach or cohort views. These boundaries help identify where a RAG assistant could retrieve product explanations without replacing application logic.

The team evaluated generative models in A6 and A7 using Beacon tasks such as screening written answers, extracting skills from resumes, summarizing practice, generating a weekly plan, and predicting readiness. The provided model-selection notebook includes Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 in the Large category and reports that it returned valid JSON on the tested matrix. The P1-A8 RAG comparison should keep this generation model fixed while changing only the embedding model and chunking method. That isolates retrieval-side changes from generation-model changes and makes the nine configurations more directly comparable.

The team's prior model study measured structure, instruction adherence, accuracy, clarity, latency, and model footprint. It found that larger models did not always beat smaller ones in every task or prompt pair, and it documented diminishing returns between the Medium and Large categories. The system-design document also reports that the top-scoring model is not always the best quality-per-second choice and that prompt-injection resistance must be treated as a gate rather than averaged into a quality score. These findings motivate a controlled RAG study: embedding dimension alone should not be assumed to predict retrieval quality, answer quality, or total latency.

Beacon routes AI features through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint configured through environment variables. The README identifies UIUC NCSA Lumen as the recommended provider when LUMEN_API_KEY is configured, and it supports other compatible providers through LLM_API_KEY, LLM_BASE_URL, and LLM_MODEL. It also describes a slower free keyless public model option when neither provider key is set. LLM_ENABLED=false disables AI calls and activates rules-based fallbacks. Secrets are kept in the local environment file, which is ignored by Git. This provider interface allows the application to change the serving endpoint without rewriting every AI feature.

Beacon presents itself as private by default and makes reminders opt-in. The README places reminder controls under the user's personal settings and describes a daily management command for sending reminders. Real email delivery requires configuring the site URL and email environment values; in development, messages are printed to the console. The product's security module handles rate limits, brute-force lockout, content security policy, and response headers, while the support area maintains an append-only audit trail. A RAG service should preserve these principles by avoiding unnecessary exposure of candidate resumes or interview responses and by applying authentication, authorization, and rate limits around retrieval endpoints.

A Beacon deployment serving ten thousand daily users should separate the web application from resource-intensive AI work. The existing system-design analysis estimates five AI jobs per active user per day for its earlier workload, or roughly fifty thousand requests per day at ten thousand daily users; that is an A7 planning assumption, not a measurement of the new RAG feature. A scalable RAG design can cache document embeddings, avoid re-embedding unchanged paragraphs, batch query embeddings, keep a persistent vector index, and queue generation requests when demand peaks. Monitoring should track retrieval latency, generation latency, queue depth, error rates, and evidence quality while keeping private candidate data under access control.
